CONGRANT.TITLE: The Cross-Border Threat Detection and Supply Chain Defense (CBTS) Center of Excellence
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) proposes the establishment of the Cross-Border Threat Screening and Supply Chain Defense (CBTS) as a Center of Excellence of the
Department of Homeland Security. In support, the vision of the CBTS COE at UTRGV is to be on the cutting edge of research and function at the frontline of operations that support the mission of the DHS by promoting and carrying out impactful and relevant research through a coalition of partners committed to homeland security. The center is committed to developing products, processes, and programs that comply with the needs and demands of DHS.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Innovation Driven Education Pathways for Defense Oriented Advanced Manufacturing Engineering (IDREAM4D)
Symbolic CAD for Tracking Student Design Evolution
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Mechanical designs are represented by solid model files in a CAD system.  Most mechanical designs are performed by engineers trained at universities. During the CAD learning process, solid models are created by students, and student creation of files occur in a step by step basis.  By capturing the evolution of these files, step by step, using human readable symbolic representation, the investigators believe important data about CAD based design evolution can be obtained to monitor design intention as well as fluency in solid modeling. This proposed study attempts to better understand design through the medium of CAD design evolution by developing symbolic representation of design evolution in a CAD system

CONGRANT.TITLE: "An Expert Systems Approach to Feature Recognition for Marine ROV Operation with Virtual Reality"
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
During the Summer of 2017, the MSI (Minority Serving Institution) team collaborated with a Maritime Security Center (MSC) Summer Research Institute (SRI) team at Stevens Institute of Technology to develop a low-cost Virtual Reality interface to assist with the operation of an ROV (Remote Operated Vehicle) for maritime homeland security applications.  The proposed research extends this work by adding an expert system for feature recognition to assist with the operation of marine ROVs.  Expertise is provided by Dr. Englot from the MSC at Stevens Institute to the U. of Texas-Rio Grande Valley team, and this expertise is used to develop an expert system that can recognize features such as contraband (drugs, etc.) and IEDs (Improvised Explosive Devices) that may attached to the hull of ships or placed underwater on pier pilings or other harbor structures.  The methods include classic expert system techniques including: the development of software to manipulate the expertise and interface with the user, elicitation of expertise from a human expert (Dr. Englot), testing of the expert system performance, and documentation of results with the intention to transition this work to an operational application of interest to relevant DHS components.
Through the development and demonstration of this VR (Virtual Reality) system with expert feature recognition, new capabilities are developed that directly support US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) efforts to keep our ports and harbors safe, and eliminate the smuggling of contraband (drugs, etc.).  Currently, ROVs have a significantly poor man-machine interface, and this research offers an opportunity to begin to correct this deficiency, providing better security for our homeland.

CONGRANT.TITLE: "Cost and Schedule Modeling in Shipbuilding"
CONGRANT.SPONORG: Office of Naval Research, STTR Program
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
NOTE THIS IS A WHITE PAPER
This white paper proposes development of cost and schedule models in shipbuilding.  Cost and schedule overruns have a very negative effect on the ship acquisition process, and by the development of an accurate and easy to use, computer-based model, managers in the shipyard and in the government can make better decisions which can help to avoid cost and schedule overruns.  To accomplish this goal, a three stage process is proposed where 1) a micro-level model is developed for work packages where the work packages are at the ship module or block level, 2) data from the micro-level model is used to develop a macro-level model applicable to an entire ship, and 3) the macro level model is extended to predict cost and schedule for the entire ship class.  Using this three step process, improved cost and schedule information becomes available to both the shipbuilder and the government, resulting in lower cost ships delivered on time.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Innovation Driven Education Pathway for Defense Oriented Advanced Manufacturing Engineering
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The success of the defense industry relies heavily on its innovation capability and its
ability for developing new systems, processes and materials that support innovation needs. While
the challenges facing the defense industry have moved on to a new level in this era, the public
perception of manufacturing remains as not interesting, less rewarding, low tech, dirty and less
secure. This poor perception comes with a lack of interest from young people and a significant gap
of talents needed to drive manufacturing innovation. This proposed project, a joint effort
collaboration of a defense lab, 5 education institutions geographically dispersed across North
America, and 8 defense manufacturers in the U.S. aims to reverse this gap though cultivating an
innovation driven manufacturing education system with instruction covering the total
manufacturing engineering enterprise. The project is designed to attract, engage, train and educate
talent to drive manufacturing and advance manufacturing technologies needed for the future of US
manufacturing and the defense industries.
To accomplish this agenda, a consortium led by the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
(UTRGV) and including, the University of Texas Austin (UT Austin), the University of Texas San
Antonio (UTSA), Virginia State University (Virginia State) and Michigan State University (MSU)
partner with the Army Research Laboratory (ARL) and industry collaborators including the United
Launch Alliance (ULA), Boeing, Ingalls Shipbuilding, Raytheon, StandardAero, Honeywell,
Navistar, and Intrex Aerospace. This geographically distributed team also includes high schools,
typically local to a university, and Career and Technical Education (CTEs) organizations to
provide both secondary and post-secondary activities to generate a pathway system.
Activities that are undertaken to support this pathway include: a research exchange program which
includes student joint supervision with ARL, preparation of Manufacturing Engineers to join and
lead defense industries including development of a defense manufacturing engineering
concentration, a defense and summer research program, a faculty exchange program, a summer
innovation camp for high school students, and student manufacturing exposure programs to assist
with student recruiting. As a result of responding to these multiple goals with corresponding
actions, the consortium team meets the needs of the multiple constituencies that it serves. Students
have a pathway from high school to an assignment in advanced manufacturing for defense
industries, and the industries have a direct opportunity to attract and hire qualified technical talent.
Our proposal focuses on Innovative Advanced Manufacturing and specifically on Systems and
Materials, and Additive Manufacturing Technologies which are capable of producing lightweight
structures and materials. This tightly targeted approach has been encouraged by ARL, our military
laboratory partner, and the defense industry partners in our consortium: Boeing, Raytheon,
Honeywell, Ingalls Shipbuilding, United Launch Alliance, and others.

CONGRANT.TITLE: "Using Low Cost, Commercially Available Virtual Environments to Reduce Shipyard Worker Time for Piping System Fabrication"
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Due to market forces in the entertainment industry, the cost of Head Mounted Display (HMD) immersive, virtual reality systems have fallen dramatically.  This provides an excellent opportunity to use these “high tech” but low cost systems to reduce shipyard worker cognitive load for fabrication tasks.  With conventional methods the shipyard worker must completely and unambiguously understand the design requirements from 2D media; whereas, with an immersive, virtual environment the worker is provided with a “like real” sensory presentation allowing a much more rapid understanding of the designer’s intent.  So, the central hypothesis of this proposed project is that the worker’s understanding can be improved and the cognitive load on the worker correspondingly reduced by the use of a low cost, commercially available virtual environment.  This reduction in worker cognitive load translates directly in to reduced worker time to complete a fabrication task.

CONGRANT.TITLE: “Virtual Reality Applications in Maritime and Port Security”
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: We propose to research the applications of virtual reality to maritime and port security.  The potential applications of virtual reality (VR) hardware to increase maritime domain awareness and to enhance the response capabilities of homeland security practitioners are numerous.  The proposed research project explores a range of applications, including but not limited to, the use of VR to visualize imaging sonar data collected from remotely operated vehicles (ROV’s).  An example may include operations in which ROV’s are used to perform ship hull and pier piling inspections to search for parasitic devices.  Through the visualization of what an ROV would see underwater and the 3-D experience of the VR, the ROV operators can enhance skills and better prepare themselves for conducting inspections in a range of underwater environments (e.g. cloudy water, rough currents, narrow and constrained spaces, etc.).  VR environments created through this research, can also assist operators to assess the effectiveness of integrated sensors (e.g. positional sensors, imaging sensors and cameras used for underwater mapping) from the location and view point of an ROV.  This VR research project leverages the hardware and software assets available in the Sensory Computation, Experimental Narrative Environments (SCENE) Lab at Stevens Institute of Technology.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Symbolic Representation of Design Evolution Using a CAD System
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Mechanical designs are represented by solid model files in a CAD system.  Most mechanical designs are performed by engineers trained at universities. During the CAD learning process, solid models are created by students, and student creation of files occur in a step by step basis.  By capturing the evolution of these files, step by step, using human readable symbolic representation, the investigators believe important data about CAD based design evolution can be obtained to monitor design intention as well as fluency in solid modeling. This proposed study attempts to better understand design through the medium of CAD design evolution by developing symbolic representation of design evolution in a CAD system.

CONGRANT.TITLE: "Evaluating the Effectiveness of Immersive Interfaces for Combat Training"
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This proposal focuses directly on immersive science.  It answers basic questions about interfaces and their characteristics with respect to human responses with these interfaces.  In this context, it studies immersion and the measurement of presence as it relates to the virtual world paradigm.  Additionally, this proposal answers questions regarding effectiveness of virtual worlds versus traditional training, as posed by an Army laboratory and a Marine Corps program office.  As part of this proposal, an Immersive Environments laboratory is established at The University of Texas-Pan American (UTPA).  At the heart of this proposal are quantitative measures of human subject responses to differences in immersive interfaces and virtual world training regimens.  Physiological measurements and statistical methods are employed to reach conclusions regarding presence in immersive environments and the effectiveness of virtual world paradigms as it relates to support for combat operations.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: A Quantitative Competitive Study of Virtual World Language Learning Compared to Classical Classroom Training
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Proceedings of EDULEARN24
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
This paper examines the effectiveness of the Alelo (TLT) package for teaching Tactical French for the Sahel Africa compared with the traditional modality of classroom language teaching with an instructor at the college level. The role of the educator in learning is a topic of debate between followers of psychologists Jean Piaget and Lev Vygotsky. Piaget (1980) believed that people learn by being immersed in an environment and that knowledge is accumulated from “a structuring activity on the part of the subject.” Piaget believes that learners are individualistic in their learning process and not dependent on a teacher or tutor. On the contrary, Vygotsky believes that the tutor’s role “is central to the learning process (Levy, 1998).
In a modern sense, Piaget’s view on individual learning is represented by a computer program from Alelo company. This computer program uses voice recognition software and simulated scenarios to provide feedback to a user attempting to learn a new language. The Vygotskian view is represented by a traditional classroom environment. The Alelo TLT System for the French language followed the previous computer-based systems produced by Alelo as a blend of human-computer interaction technology and task-based language techniques. The learner engages by clicking the microphone icon and speaking into the headset microphone.
To compare the effectiveness of virtual environment training provided by Alelo to that of a traditional classroom, a teacher is needed to properly teach the material to the class. Using the Alelo software, the teacher created 110 questions. From these questions, the teacher created two 20-question exams with the same format and the same level of difficulty. In addition to creating the exams, the teacher teaches the class for the group of subjects learning Sub-Saharan French in a traditional classroom environment with the same material the Alelo virtual environments software covers, with the same time restrictions as the students using the Alelo software, ten hours of instruction over three days. After the experiment is complete, the teacher grades each subject’s pre-test and post-test and reports the grades for analysis. The study includes two groups with n = 31 for the Alelo group and n = 33 for the classical group to compare exam results through a test of hypothesis.
Analysis of these scores consists of three parts: testing if either method effectively improved the subjects’ French language proficiency, testing if one class type performed better than the other, and testing if the improvement in scores is correlated to any experimental factors (i.e. gender, subject number, and days to complete testing). With a p-value of 0.309, no significant difference was found between the performance of the two test groups. This paper uses a pre-test and post-test regimen on a competitive basis with two approximately equal samples totaling 64 subjects. This quantitative comparative study reaches conclusions at the 95% confidence level using rigorous statistical methods.
Therefore, the hypothesis that the two educational methods were equal cannot be statistically rejected. The result of this experiment is there is no significant difference between the effect the Alelo training had on the subjects’ performance and the effect the classroom training had on the subjects’ performance. However, both training types effectively improved the subjects’ proficiency in French.

Computer Assisted Language Learning, Alelo, Educational Technology, E-learning, Virtual Worlds

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: This paper investigates the hypothesis that men and women perform differently in virtual environments in terms of balance and coordination during surprise events. It reports on an experiment in human subject balance and coordination using an HTC Vive head-mounted display (HMD) to create a virtual environment. For the experiment, 30 male and 30 female subjects of college age were asked to navigate along a clear path in a virtual world using a controller with their dominant hand and asked to balance a virtual ball on a virtual plate using the other controller in the nondominant hand. The test subjects moved along a clearly marked path, with three surprise obstacles occurring: a large rock landing near the path, an explosion near the path, and a flock of birds coming across the path. Data included six degrees-of-freedom (DOF) trajectories for the head and both hands, as well as data gathered by the computer system on ball location and velocity, plate location and velocity, and ball status. Likert scale questionnaires were answered by the test subjects relative to video game experience, sense of presence, and ease of managing the ball movement. Statistics showed that the male students dropped the ball less frequently at p = 0.0254 and p = 0.0036. In contrast, female students were aware of their performance with correlation levels of 0.632 and 0.588.
